query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys intended for high-temperature applications, the formation of a defective interfacial buffer layer (such as an oxygen- or carbon-vacancy rich layer) during rapid laser synthesis governs the structural and chemical stability. This buffer layer restricts atomic diffusion and mitigates phase segregation despite the high thermal energy, thereby preserving the homogeneous solid-solution state.
generation.material_initial_state: Ultra-fine, equimolar high-entropy nanoalloys synthesized via a pulsed laser-induced thermionic emission process on a carbonaceous support, exhibiting a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the nanoalloys to prolonged high-temperature annealing (e.g., 400–800 °C) to simulate operational conditions.
generation.conditions: Annealing under controlled inert or mildly reactive environments, across a temperature range of approximately 400 °C to 800 °C over timescales of up to several hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A defective interfacial layer (characterized by vacancies and structural disruptions on the nanoparticle surface) provided by the support and/or formed during the rapid synthesis process.
generation.mechanism: The defective interfacial layer acts as a diffusion barrier by accommodating strain and inhibiting atomic rearrangements that lead to phase segregation. Its presence sustains high configurational entropy by restricting atom mobility, thus maintaining the metastable solid-solution state even under high thermal exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoalloys featuring the defective interfacial buffer layer will retain a nearly homogeneous composition and single-phase structure after high-temperature treatment, whereas nanoalloys lacking such an interfacial mediator (e.g., those synthesized on an inert support) will display signs of diffusion, elemental segregation, and phase transformation.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloys synthesized on non-defective inert supports that lack the formation of an interfacial buffer layer, which are expected to show increased phase segregation and compositional inhomogeneity upon high-temperature annealing.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is predicted to be most effective for nanoalloys with particle sizes in the 1–3 nm range and under heat treatments up to about 800 °C for durations typical of laboratory-scale high-temperature applications. Behavior outside these size or temperature/time ranges may involve additional kinetic or thermodynamic effects.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of the interfacial defective layer in impeding diffusion is expected, the quantitative limits (e.g., exact temperature thresholds, degree of defectiveness required, and specific diffusion coefficients) remain uncertain due to the complex interplay between nanoscale effects and thermal dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples: (1) synthesized via pulsed laser ablation on a carbonaceous support designed to generate a defective interfacial layer, and (2) synthesized on an inert oxide support that minimizes interfacial defect formation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing protocols (e.g., 400–800 °C for several hours).
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to map elemental distribution and detect phase segregation.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to determine phase purity and crystal structure stability before and after annealing.
Surface-sensitive techniques such as X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to characterize the presence and nature of interfacial defects.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoalloys on both supports exhibit similar degrees of atomic diffusion, phase segregation, and loss of homogeneous structure after annealing, thereby showing no significant difference attributable to the presence of a defective interfacial layer, then the hypothesis that such a layer governs high-temperature stability would be falsified.

(Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Realistic microstructure evolution of complex Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr high-entropy alloys by simulation techniques

Abstract: Over last 15 years high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) have gained much appreciation for their numerous superior properties. In this paper we have shown a novel simulation methodology to realistically predict the nanometer level local structural features of complex Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25 HEA. This involves prediction of the morphology of the short-range clustering (SRCs), their quantitative atomic composition at the nano level and the thermodynamic aspects. An alloy structure model containing 11664 atoms was created and this was subjected to structure evolution at 1800 °C. The structure evolution technique is based on a combined hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics (MC/MD) approach. Nanoalloy libraries from laser-induced thermionic emission reduction

Abstract: Nanoalloys, especially high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) that contain equal stoichiometric metallic elements in each nanoparticle, are widely used in vast applications. Currently, the synthesis of HENAs is challenged by slow reaction kinetics that leads to phase segregation, sophisticated pretreatment of precursors, and inert conditions that preclude scalable fabrication of HENAs. Here, we report direct conversion of metal salts to ultrafine HENAs on carbonaceous support by nanosecond pulsed laser under atmospheric conditions. Because of the unique laser-induced thermionic emission and etch on carbon, the reduced metal elements were gathered to ultrafine HENAs and stabilized by defective carbon support. This scalable, facile, and low-cost method overcomes the immiscible issue and can produce various HENAs uniformly with a size of 1 to 3 nanometers and metal elements up to 11 with productivity up to 7 grams per hour.
